Send men, therefore, and whatever pleases you from my father’s treasures, I will send to you with good will.” King Clodoneus wrote back to him: “I give thanks for your good will; I ask that you reveal everything to our men when they come, since you alone are henceforth to possess your father’s kingdom with our friendship.”

When the envoys of King Clodoneus came, Ludovicus showed them his father’s treasures. While they were inspecting various and diverse things, the young man said: “In this chest my father was accustomed to store gold coins.” “Put your hand in,” one of those standing by said, “all the way to the bottom, so that you may test whether it is all gold.” When he had done this and was bent far down, the very man who had ordered it raised his hand and swung an axe into his brain; he died at once in that same place.
When these wicked deeds had been done, King Clodoneus came to Cologne, and, as if unaware of the crimes, summoned all the people of the city and said:

“Listen, excellent citizens, to the unspeakable evil that lately occurred. [Chloderic?], the son of my kinsman Sigebert, ensnared his father with false words, saying that I was plotting against his life. And when he was fleeing through the [Buconian?] forest, robbers were sent against him, and he killed his own father. He too, while he was brooding over the treasures, was struck by someone I know not and perished. But in these matters I am in no way privy to the crime. For I cannot shed the blood of my kinsmen, since it is a sin.”

But because these things had so happened, “I give you counsel, if it seems acceptable: turn yourselves to me, so that you may be under my protection.” And they, applauding with hands and voices, set him up on a raised shield according to the custom of the nation, and appointed him king over them. And thus he received into his own power the kingdom of Sigebert with all his treasures. For God daily laid his enemies low beneath his hands, and greatly increased his kingdom, because he walked with an upright heart in the way of God’s commandments.

He also deceitfully seized King Chararic and his son; first tonsuring them, he had one ordained priest and the other deacon. Subjecting their treasures together with the kingdom to himself, he afterwards had both their heads cut off.

[Ragnachar?] also, the king ruling the Franks at Cambrai and living far too wantonly and luxuriously, together with Richarius his brother, were treacherously captured while fleeing from battle; striking them with an axe by his own hand, he killed them.
He also had [Rignomer?], their brother, who was reigning at Le Mans, killed with similar cruelty.

When these men had died, he usurped their kingdoms with their treasures for himself. He also killed many other kings of the Franks, all of whom had been begotten from the blood of his own kin, especially those of whom he was suspiciously very much afraid, lest they take the kingdom away from him; sparing no one, and in this way, when almost all his kinsmen had been extinguished, he enlarged his kingdom throughout all Gaul. But let Hunibald praise Clodoneus as much as he wished, as though he had done well in these matters: I, in this respect, cannot praise a parricide, and one who killed so many innocent men.

For on a certain day, in the presence of many of his courtiers, he is said to have spoken about these relatives and kinsmen of his, whom he himself had destroyed: “Woe to me, because, like a foreigner among strangers, I remain alone, and today I have no one of my relatives or kinsmen still living who could help me in any way in adversity, if it should come upon me, as friend is accustomed to help friend.” But he said this deceitfully, thinking that someone from among those standing around would answer by way of consolation: “Behold, you still have this man or that man from among your own [unclear],” so that those of his kinsmen who survived might themselves also be killed as quickly as possible.

In the seventeenth year of his reign, King Clodoneus, at the continual urging of Queen Clotild, who desired the cruel death of her parents to be avenged upon her paternal uncle, declared war on Gundebald, king of the Burgundians. When he had been defeated, Clodoneus assigned Burgundy to the tribute and subjection of the Franks.
The fictitious exculpation of King Clodoneus.
The people of Cologne receive Clodoneus as king.
Chararic and his son, kings, killed by Clodoneus through deceit.
[Ragnachar?], king of Cambresian Francia, is killed with his brother.
[Rignomer?], king of Cenomannian Francia, is killed by him.
There were several kings of the Franks in these times.
To reign by wronging one’s kin is cruelty.
The words of King Clodoneus were spoken deceitfully.
No one doubts [that he was] an evil man.
War of the Franks against the Burgundians.
Clodoneus, king of the Franks, dies.

Clodoneus, king of the Franks, after his realm had been extended throughout all Gaul and a great part of Germany, and after many things had been bravely accomplished in war and peace, at last died in the thirtieth year of his reign, the fifty-first of his age, and the year of the Lord’s nativity 514, in the seventh Roman indiction. He was buried at Paris in the church of Saint Peter.

He left four sons: Lotharius, Theodoricus, Clodomirus, and Hildebertus, who divided their father’s kingdom in equal portions. But because several kings were subsequently born from these men, and because at one time the kingdom of the Franks was subject to a single monarch, while at another time it was divided into several parts and ruled by many, we have judged it worth the effort to continue in order, marked chapter by chapter in red, the names of those kings who carried the sequence of the royal stock in a direct line down to Hildericus, the last king. For among the sons of Clodoneus, Lotharius was not the firstborn; rather Theodoricus was the elder by birth. Clodomirus was born second; Lotharius himself, by whom the genealogy of the kings is continued, was born third.

After King Clodoneus died, Hunibald also completed his history of the origin of the Franks, divided into eighteen books, comprising a period of no fewer than nine hundred and fifty years, in which there were forty-seven kings from Marcomirus, son of Antenor, who first led the people from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the river Rhine in Germany, down to the death of King Clodoneus. What follows in this second volume of our annals we have taken from authors whose names are these.

Einhardus, abbot of Saint-Amand; Flodoardus, priest of the church of Reims; Richerus, monk of Reims; Gregorius, archbishop of Tours; Lampertus, abbot in Hasungen; Regino, abbot of Prum; Eghardus, first abbot in Vraugia; Lampertus, monk of Hersfeld; Freculfus, formerly a monk, bishop of Lisieux; Strabus, monk of Fulda; Vuindekindus, monk in Corvey of Saxony; Rupertus, monk of Saint Alban near Mainz; Ioannes, monk of the same monastery; Adelbertus, monk of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz; Meginfridus, monk of Fulda; Golftherus, monk of Saint Matthias, in the deeds of the Treveri; Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda; Sigebertus, monk of Gembloux; Richardus, monk of Cluny; Rupertus Ganguinus also, formerly minister general of the Order of the Holy Trinity; Ado, bishop of Vienne; Galfridus Brito; Saxo Dacus; Ptolemaeus of Lucca, a Saxon by country, in the Rudimentum novitiorum; Vuernherus, Carthusian monk of Cologne; Gotfridus of Viterbo; Rupertus, Premonstratensian canon; Hartmannus Schedel from Nuremberg; Iacobus of Bergamo, hermit of Saint Augustine; Marcus Antonius Sabellicus. From the aforementioned and various other writers of histories I wrote the two volumes of our annals that follow, not without the greatest labor, because there is much diversity among historiographers, not only in the years,

Historiographers. Einhardus. Flodoardus. Richerus. Gregorius. Lampertus. Regino, abbot. Eghardus. Lampertus. Freculfus, bishop. Strabus. Vuindekindus. Rupertus. Ioannes, monk. Ammonius. Adelbertus. Megnifridus. Golfcherus. Marianus. Sigebertus. Richardus. Rupertus. Ado, bishop. Galfredus. Saxo [unclear]. Ptolemaeus. Vuernherus. Godfridus. Rupertus. Hartmannus. Iacobus of Bergamo. Marcus A. Helinandus. Vincentius. Antonius. Martinus. Andreas M.

but also in the deeds and names of persons, which has increased my labor not a little, since quite often something is ascribed to one person which another did or said, and something that was done in another year is narrated as having been done in this one, and a deed which was done in this way by one is said by another to have been done otherwise.

Since, therefore, it is not within my powers to reconcile so great a discordance of histories, I follow the judgment of those whom I find to have differed less from one another, which could be observed not uniformly in every case, but in certain cases.

Therefore the third-born son of King Clodoveus, from whom the line of the kings of the Franks descending in direct succession continued down to Hilderic, the last of the stock of Faramund, reigned after his father in Soissons, a city of the Franks, for fifty years; and when his brothers and all their sons had died, he finally recalled into one monarchy the kingdom that had been divided into four parts. Each of his brothers reigned for a time in his own place.
There is great disagreement among the historians.
Trithemius follows those less discordant.
The Forty-Eighth.
Lotharius reigns for fifty years.

¶ For Theodoricus, the first-born of King Clodoveus, whom he had begotten not by Queen Clotildis, but before his marriage to her by a certain concubine, received in the division of the kingdom of the Franks Austrasia, in which is the city of Metz, together with the other cities belonging to it; and at that time it was called the kingdom of Austrasia, or of the Austrasians, in which he reigned for twenty-three years. After him Theodobertus, his son, reigned over the Austrasians for twenty-two years. When he too had died, his son Theodobaldus reigned over the people of Metz for nine years; and when he had departed this life, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 560, in the eighth Roman indiction, without children, his uncle Lotharius, named above, received the kingdom of the Austrasians, or of the people of Metz.
Theodoricus reigned over the Austrasians for twenty-three years.
Theodobertus reigns after his father for [fourteen?] years.
Theodobaldus reigns for nine years.

¶ Clodomirus, however, the third son of Clodoveus, but the first-born by Queen Clotildis, reigned at Orléans in Gaul for seven years; and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 521, after he had killed Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, with his wife and sons, and had again engaged with his brother Godemarus, he was killed by him. He left three young sons, Theodobaldus, Guntherus, and Clodoaldus; after their father’s death, the most pious grandmother Clotildis, living at Tours, raised them with herself like a mother. But a few years later, Lotharius and Hildebertus, kings and brothers of the aforesaid Clodomirus, having summoned to themselves their nephews Theodobaldus and Guntharius, and in their ambition for rule devising wicked things, killed them with their own hands. But the third, changing nobility destined to perish into divine servitude, became a cleric.
Clodomirus reigned at Orléans for seven years.
The three sons of King Clodomirus of Orléans are named.
The impious kings killed their nephews.

¶ Hildebertus, however, the fourth son of Clodoveus, king of the Franks, received the kingdom of Neustria in the division of the monarchy, and reigned at Paris for forty-six years. When he at last died, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 559, in the seventh Roman indiction, his brother Lotharius received the kingdom of the Parisians into his own power. Thus, with three now
Hildebertus reigned in Neustria for forty-five years.
H

Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, killed his son. King Sigismund performed great penance. Bertharius and Baldaricus, kings of the Thuringians, are slain. Ermenfrid, king of Thuringia, had the brothers treacherously killed. Saint Brigid died in Scotland. Boethius, the consul, a most learned man, died. Saint Benedict, father of monks. He wrote the Rule of monks. The Order of Saint Benedict is instituted. The Cistercian. Also the Celestines, Wilhelmites, Mount Olivet, the Slavs, Vallombrosa, Saint Paul, the Humiliati. The expedition of the Franks into Thuringia. The final destruction of the kingdom of the Thuringians by the Franks.

With the brothers and their sons and grandsons dead, or cruelly killed, Lothar alone obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter, after all his brothers, reigned still for five years.

In the second year of King Lothar, Sigismund, king of Burgundy, who had built the monastery of the Agaunensian martyrs, killed his son Sigeric, having followed the wicked counsel of that boy’s stepmother. Led to great penitence, he devoted himself wholly to the holy martyrs of Agaunum; and that he was worthy of pardon is attested by frequent miracles after his death, for in his honor health is granted to those suffering from fever.

In the fourth year of King Lothar, Theodoric, king of Austrasia, his brother, having been asked by Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, under the promise of half his kingdom, treacherously killed the brothers Bertharius and Balderic on the road, while they were returning toward Thuringia, suspecting no evil, from the city of Metz, to which they had come for the sake of greeting him. But when the crime had been carried out, and Theodoric sought from Ermenfrid the half of the kingdom of Thuringia promised to him, the latter neither gave what he had promised nor sent a fitting reply to the petitioner, deceived by the counsel of his wife, who was the sister of that Theodoric and of Lothar. This matter afterward, as we have said in the first volume of the Annals, brought on the final destruction of all Thuringia and extinguished there the royal name and title. In the same year the holy virgin Brigid, dying in Scotland, ascended to Christ.

In the seventh year of Lothar, king of the Franks, Boethius, the Roman consul, worn down by long imprisonment, was killed by Theodoric, king of the Goths, who, after Odoacer had been slain, was occupying Italy; he wrote many useful works for the faith of Christ. Father Benedict, our holy lawgiver, also flourished in these times in Italy, the first founding abbot of the monastery of Cassino, who was the prince of all western monks. To them he handed down a rule of life outstanding in every discretion, and a lucid teaching of words, made honorable by his deeds, is called by the name of Saint Benedict himself. The Order of Cistercian monks also professes the same rule. The Order of Saint William. The Order of Mount Olivet. The Order of the Slavs. The Order of Vallombrosa. The Order of Saint Paul the First Hermit. The Order of the Humiliati, together with certain others which, for the sake of brevity, we have passed over here. The life of this saint the divine Pope Gregory set forth.

In the tenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 524, the seventh indiction of the Romans, when the king of the people of Metz sought satisfaction from Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, for the murder of his brother, as we have said, and did not obtain it, he was roused to anger. Having called to his aid his son Theudebert and his brother Lothar, kings, he moved an expedition into Thuringia, captured King Ermenfrid with his wife and children, and subjected the whole kingdom to himself.
From that time the Thuringians did not have a king of their own.

And Radegund, among the other captives, daughter of Bertharius, once king, whom, as we have said, his brother Ermenfrid had caused to be killed through Theodoric king of the Metensians, King Lotharius joined to himself in marriage. She shone with great holiness, and afterward, becoming a nun, was radiant with very many signs and miracles. Concerning this destruction of the Thuringians, Fortunatus the archbishop wrote more fully in verse and in prose.

In the twelfth year of his reign, Lotharius king of the Franks, with his brother Hildebert, besieged Autun, a city of Burgundy, and, after King Godomar had been put to flight, powerfully subjected the whole province of the Burgundians to his rule.
In the year [unclear] of the reign of Lotharius king of the Franks, he powerfully wrested from the hand of King Athalaric whatever his grandfather Theodoric, king of Italy, had possessed in Gaul.

In these days Saint Nicetius flourished, formerly abbot of the monastery of Limoges, archbishop of Trier, a man of many virtues in Christ, whose deeds are extant. Theodoric king of Austrasia, who ruled over the Metensians, the people of Trier, Liege, Cologne, Mainz, and all those dwelling this side of the Rhine, brought many clerics from among the Arvernian citizens, whom he ordered to be enrolled for service to the Lord in the church of Trier.

In the twenty-sixth year of King Lotharius, in the ninth indiction, King Hildebert, with his brother’s son Theodobert, rose against that same Lotharius, his brother. But his mother Clotild, by prayers before God, acting so that there should be no war among her sons, they were restrained by a dreadful storm; and since not even a sign of so great a terror appeared over Lotharius, Hildebert, compelled by manifest necessity, withdrew from his brother in peace.

In the twenty-eighth year, Lotharius and Hildebert, the aforementioned brothers, after besieging the city of Caesaraugusta in Spain, when the citizens prayed to God and carried around the tunic of the holy martyr Vincent, received from them as a gift the stole of that martyr himself, and returned in peace, after the greater part of Spain had been acquired by war. At the same time Saint Maurus and Faustus, disciples of the divine Benedict, flourished in Gallic France, distinguished in conduct, learning, holiness of life, and miracles.

In the fortieth year of Lotharius king of the Franks, and in the year 554 of the Lord’s nativity, in the second Roman indiction, Queen Clotild died, formerly the wife of the great Clovis, king of France, with whom she also was buried at Paris in the church of Saint Peter. In the same year Bucellinus and Amingus, dukes of the Franks, having joined battle with Narses the Roman patrician, were both killed by him, together with not a few others.

For these were the two dukes Bucellinus and Amingus, who seven years earlier had entered Italy with Theodobert, king of the Franks, with a strong force, and did not cease to disturb it with various warlike assaults. From there, sailing into Sicily, they subjected it to the tribute of the Franks, and, after many spoils had been gathered, rebellion [unclear]
In the forty-third year of his reign, Lotharius king of the Franks, having gathered his forces, moved into Saxony. For the Saxons, until then tributary to the Franks, into rebellion

Lotharius alone obtained the monarchy. King Lotharius burned Chramn, his son, with fire. Lotharius, king of the Franks, dies. The monastery of Saint Medard is built at Soissons. The monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Pres is founded.

The Forty-Ninth. Chilperic reigned twenty-four years. Two years earlier he reigned at Soissons. Audovera, wife of King Chilperic. Fredegund, deceiver of the queen. The contriver of the deceit addresses the king. Chilperic repudiates Audovera as his co-mother.

They rise up, and the Thuringians too bring aid, who themselves also bore the yoke of the Franks with great hardship and, with equal firmness, refused every tribute. Therefore Lotharius, coming into Saxony with a great army, subdued the Saxons in a severe battle.

In the forty-fifth year of his reign, Lotharius the king, now that his brother Childebert was dead, and all the others, both his nephews and his brothers, had either been killed or consumed by natural death, alone obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks for five years.

In the forty-ninth year of his reign Lotharius, king of the Franks, pursued with an army Chramn, his son, long rebellious and doing many evil things in the kingdom, when he had fled into New Brittany, which was formerly called Armorica, to Conobrus, duke of Brittany. When battle was joined, he killed Duke Conobrus, obtained Brittany, captured his son, and, consumed by fires together with his wife and daughters, reduced him to ashes.

In the following year, that is, the fiftieth of his reign, but the year of the Lord’s nativity 563, in the twelfth indiction of the Romans, this same Lotharius, king of the Franks, dies, leaving four sons, Charibert, Gunthram, Sigebert, and Chilperic, who again divided their father’s kingdom among themselves. The aforesaid King Lotharius built the abbey of Saint Medard, formerly the first bishop of Noyon and Tournai, at Soissons, into which he translated the body of the same saint from Tournai and placed it with the highest reverence and honor. But King Childebert, his brother, built the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Pres, in which he deposited the stole of Saint Vincent the martyr together with his dalmatic. But the order of the abridgement now requires that we pursue the division of the kingdom.

Chilperic the Younger, son of Lotharius king of the Franks, is therefore placed by us before his brothers in this abridgement of the kings, because through him the line of kings descending in straight order is continued down to Childeric. He reigned in the city of Soissons two years before the death of his father, and, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-two years. And thus the whole time that he reigned was twenty-four years. The name of his first wife was Audovera, by whom he begot two sons, Clovis and Merovech, both of whom, killed in adolescence by the deceit of their stepmother, as we said in the first volume, perished.

When Audovera had given birth to an infant while the king was absent, since no one who would raise the boy to be baptized from the sacred font was at hand, the queen mother herself, deceived by Fredegund’s wicked counsel, fulfilled the office of co-mother, and raised from baptism the infant whom she had borne. Fredegund, the contriver of the deceit, joyfully announcing this to the king when he soon came, said: “You will not have Audovera as wife henceforth, O king; she preferred to be your co-mother rather than your spouse. Now I am yours.” For this reason King Chilperic repudiated Audovera his wife, asserting that by decree of the canons it was forbidden him to have his co-mother as wife. Seduced by such cunning through Fredegund, the queen is thrust into a monastery, her
deceitful Fredegundis, by fraud, was taken by King Hilperic as his wife; by her he begot, as we shall say later, the successor to his fatherly kingdom.

Heribert, however, the eldest son of Lotharius, in the division of the monarchy of the kingdom of the Franks received Neustria, holding the seat of his kingdom at Paris; and he reigned nine years, and, doing nothing worthy of memory, died in the year of the Lord 573, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans, leaving the kingdom to his brothers.

Gunthramus, King Lotharius’s second-born son, reigned at Orleans for thirty-three years, a prince excellent in his own condition, but he obtained a most wicked wife, named Austrigildis. Among the many evils she perpetrated, when she was sick unto death and could not be helped by the physicians, she circumvented the king with crafty persuasion, so that he confirmed by an undoubted oath that he would grant her the fulfilment of one request. “Before I die,” she said, “have the heads of my physicians, who have tormented me in vain with their medicines, cut off while I am watching.” What more? Those who were to bring in the physicians were sent at once; when they entered the queen’s chamber, the witch said: “Ha! You are not physicians, but liars, who by your medicines force me to die before my time. I have prepared such a reward for you that, compelled to die, you shall pass over before me.” Soon, to satisfy the lust of the impious woman, the executioner, as ordered, cut off the heads of the two innocent physicians while that beast herself watched and laughed. King Gunthramus died in the year of the Lord 597, in the fifteenth indiction of the Romans.

Sigebert, however, the third-born son of King Lotharius, reigned at Metz in Austrasia over the people of Trier, and also those of [unclear], Cologne, Mainz, and the other cities and provinces on this side of the Rhine, for thirteen years. He had as wife a Spaniard named Brunia, whom writers have more often been accustomed to call Brunihildis, the murderess of ten kings, who was so hateful to the Franks that the prophecy of the Sibyl seemed to be fulfilled in her, saying:

“There will come Brunia from the regions of Spain; before her sight peoples and kings will perish, but she herself will perish by the heels of horses.” Hilperic begot from her a son named Theodobert, who afterward reigned twenty-one years and died in the year of the Lord 599. His son, named Theodoricus, succeeding, reigned sixteen years; at the instigation of his grandmother Brunichildis he expelled Saint Columbanus from Gaul in the year of the Lord 614, and died shortly afterward, leaving three sons, as is read, bastards. The eldest, Sigebert, was put to flight in battle by Lotharius, son of the aforesaid king, and thereafter appeared nowhere. Corbus, the second-born, was killed by the same Lotharius. But Meroveus, the third-born, whom the same Lotharius had raised from the sacred font, he preserved alive. Brunihildis, however, the murderess of ten kings, he put to death.

In the third year of King Hilperic, the Huns, having gone out with a great army, began to ravage the regions of the Franks in Thuringia in hostile fashion. Against their insolence King Sigebert, brother of King Hilperic,
Hilbert reigned nine years.
Hildebert, king of Neustria, given over to idleness.
Gunthramus reigned at Orleans thirty-three years.
A cruel queen, unworthy of memory.
The physicians are beheaded by the persuasion of the queen.
King Gunthramus dies.
Sigebert reigned in Austrasia.
Brunichildis, wife of Sigebert, cruel.
Prophecy of the Sibyl concerning Queen Brunihildis.
Theodoricus, king of Austrasia, his son.
The three sons of Theodoricus and bastards.
The Huns ravaging Thuringia are [unclear] by the Franks.
Thuringia had been subjugated by the Franks.
Battle-lines of fighting men were seen in the air. Gregory.
The Lombards came from Pannonia into Italy.
The part of the Saxons who are now Westphalians entered Italy with the Winili.
The Suevi received Saxony from King Sigebert for thirteen years.
The Winili, so called first and afterward Lombards. The Saxons were deceived by the Lombards.
The Saxons return through Gaul to their own lands.
The Suevi refused to admit the Saxons.
War takes place between the Saxons and the Suevi.
Whence the name Westphalians, who are also Lombards in Ptolemy.

under whose reign the Thuringians were contained, brought forth his forces, joined battle, laid low many thousands of the Huns, and put the rest to flight. Meanwhile, while Sigebert was occupied in Thuringia with the Huns, his brother, King Chilperic, forgetful of brotherly charity, laid waste the borders of his kingdom with a hostile incursion, and besieged the city of Reims, and received it in surrender.

In the same year spears were seen in the air, and battle-lines of soldiers, and at the same time the din of clashes was heard, first portending the incursion of the Lombards into Italy, concerning whom Pope Gregory the Great speaks in a homily. For in the following year, namely the year of the Lord’s nativity 568, in the first Roman indiction, Alboin king of the Lombards entrusted Pannonia, in which he had formerly dwelt with his people, to the Huns, friends of the Lombards, and, taking as allies Saxons, Marcomanni, and other neighboring peoples, occupied with all his people that part of Italy which, from the name of the people, is called Lombardy down to the present.

In the same year Sigebert king of the Franks, who lived at Metz in Austrasia, brother of Chilperic, surveying the land of Saxony, empty of inhabitants who had gone with the Lombards, as we have said, into Italy, lest it be reduced utterly to solitude, handed it over to the Suevi to inhabit. And so the Saxons lived with the Lombards in Italy, and the Suevi in Saxony, for fourteen years. When these had passed, since the Saxons saw themselves among the Lombards in the lowest place, in the condition of slaves, they took counsel to return to Saxony.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s nativity 582, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, the Saxons who were with the Lombards in Italy, no longer enduring the pride and unjust domination of the Winili, for so the Lombards were formerly called, returned with their children and wives, under the conduct of Sigebert king of the Franks, through southern Gaul to Cologne Agrippina. There, after crossing the Rhine, they sought again their former seats in Saxony, which they had left behind.

But the Suevi, to whom King Sigebert had given them to inhabit, at first denied the Saxons entry; secondly, they agreed to restore to them a third part. But when the Saxons demanded back not a part but the whole, the Suevi offered half the region. The Saxons remained constant in their judgment, demanding back not a part, not half of the land, but the entire whole.

At last the matter was committed to the sword; the fight for possession of the settlements was waged very fiercely by both armies. At length the Suevi were defeated; more than twenty thousand of them perished in that battle by the sword of the Saxons. And thus the Saxons recovered by war the land which, by the persuasion of the Winili, they had left quite imprudently, in the fourteenth year after their departure, some of the Suevi being killed, others expelled.

From that time the aforesaid Saxons, returning from Lombardy into Germany, are called Westphalians, that is, western Gauls, down to the present day, although they are nevertheless true Saxons and Germans. The city

they built in the middle of their region a new [city], which they called Milan, in memory of the other one in Lombardy; in it there is now the episcopal see of the church of Münster. Hence some writers also called these Saxons, or Westphalians, Lombards, because they cast off their customs and rites in Saxony.

In the fifth year of King Chilperic, the king of Austrasia, his brother, remembering the injuries which he had received from him when, in the preceding year, absent from the kingdom, he was fighting with the Huns in Thuringia, gathered a great army and advanced against him to war. He occupied the city of Soissons, the seat of his brother Chilperic’s kingdom. He condemned his son Theodebert, when captured, to exile; he defeated Chilperic himself in battle and put him to flight; and all the things which he had previously taken away he recovered again for himself, and he usurped a great part of his kingdom.
In the same year King Sigebert took as wife Bruna, or Brunhild, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Visigoths, as was said above, who was reigning in Spain.

In the seventh year of Chilperic, king of the Franks, the Huns again devastated Thuringia; by magic arts they accomplished great things. Against them Sigebert, king of the Franks, advanced to battle. By their enchantments he had almost been deceived and defeated, but, prudently invoking the name of Christ, he stood firm, fought manfully, and finally conquered; and when a treaty had been concluded, the Huns returned to their own lands.

In the following year the Winili, who are the Lombards, after the city of Pavia had been taken by surrender after a siege of three years, in a short time gained almost all Italy except Rome and Ravenna, and, with no one resisting them, held dominion powerfully everywhere. In the ninth year of King Chilperic, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, his brother Charibert died, king of the Franks, who reigned in Neustria, in the city of the Parisians, without children.

In the tenth year of Chilperic, king of the Franks, Alboin, king of the Lombards, was killed by a certain armor-bearer of his on the following occasion. In the five hundred and seventh year of the Lord’s nativity, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, in the times of Lothar, great king of the Franks, this same King Alboin had a war with Chunimund, king of the Gepids, in which sixty thousand men fell on both sides. There Alboin killed Chunimund and had a drinking-cup fitted for himself from the shell of his head, which he was especially accustomed to use on the festive days of birthdays. He also took his daughter captive as his wife. And when, in the aforesaid year of Chilperic, on a certain solemn day, having become rather merry among the cups, he offered his wife her father’s brain, saying [unclear] For two years after he had died, the Lombards were under dukes for ten years.

Chilperic, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth year of his reign, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, too treacherously presses, harasses, and disturbs Sigebert his brother, king of the Franks in Austrasia, through his son Theodebert.
The city of the Westphalians, Milan, now Münster.
The Westphalians, who are Lombard Saxons.
The war of King Sigebert against Chilperic his brother.
Bruna, who is Brunhild, becomes the wife of King Sigebert.
The Huns devastated Thuringia.
The Lombards, who are Winili, take Pavia.
Charibert, king of Neustria, died among the Parisians.
Alboin, king of the Lombards, is killed.
Chunimund, king of the Gepids, is killed.
Sixty thousand men fell in that battle.
Alboin, king of the Lombards, is killed.
Sigebert, king of the Franks, dies among the Austrasians.

Whence, in the following year, the fourteenth of King Hilperic, and the year of the Lord’s nativity 578, a cruel war arose between them, in which Theodobert, son of Hilperic, was killed, and many of the Franks were slain on both sides.

After this, the Franks over whom Hilperic ruled, holding their own lord in hatred, resolved by common counsel to set over themselves as king his brother Sigebert, who seemed to be of a gentler disposition. When Fredegund, the wife of Hilperic, learned this, she sent two boys and treacherously caused King Sigebert to be killed in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity.

In the following year Hilperic, king of the Franks, compelled Brunhild, the widow of his brother Sigebert, to go into exile with her sons. Almost all the Franks labored under hatred of this woman; although she made excessive use of much insolence, nevertheless she honored the churches of God. She also built several monasteries, and in various places established from the foundations new buildings of different kinds and of admirable workmanship.

In the seventeenth year of Hilperic, king of the Franks, the dukes of the Lombards began to lay waste the borders of the Gauls. The Franks met them with a great and strong multitude of forces, and fought several battles with them with doubtful fortune, sometimes defeated, and sometimes also victorious. In the end, however, the Franks triumphed.

Hilperic, king of the Franks, in the twenty-third year of his reign after his father, at the contrivance of his wife Fredegund, was killed in the year of the Lord’s nativity 587, in the fifth indiction of the Romans, leaving behind one only son, named Lothar the Younger, an infant of four months, who succeeded in the kingdom. The son of the husband-slaying Fredegund, when he was an infant of four months, was put in his father’s place and reigned forty-four years, beginning under the guardianship and direction of his mother. In the second year of his reign, Antharius, king of the Lombards, after the dukes had been driven out, took as wife Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of Bavaria; to her, as to a woman of singular devotion, blessed Pope Gregory afterward sent the four books of the Dialogues.

In the fifth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the tenth indiction of the Romans, Saint Gregory the First, pope, formerly a monk and deacon, was ordained at Rome. He wrote, said, and did many things for the honor and benefit of the holy Church.

In the same year also, when Antharius, king of the Lombards, had died without children, the Lombards, having granted Queen Theodelinda the choice of selecting a husband for herself and a king for Italy, chose Agilulf as king for themselves and at the same time as her husband; thereafter he ruled energetically over the Lombards for twenty-five years.

In the eighth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth indiction of the Romans, Garibald, king of the Bavarians, died, the father of the aforementioned Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards. After him Hildebert, king of the Franks, appointed as king of Bavaria a certain duke named Thassido, born of the race of the Franks, who overcame the Forabos, who are Slavs but later were called Bohemians, in war.

In the following year King Agilulf entered, intending to lay waste the borders of the Romans; but through the action of Theodolinda, queen of the Lombards, who was the wife of that same Agilulf, as we have said, not long afterward he made a treaty of friendship with them. Nevertheless, entering the monastery of our holy father Benedict the abbot on Monte Cassino, they plundered and destroyed it, the monks at that same time fleeing to Rome.

In the tenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, in the fifteenth indiction, Gunthram, king of the Franks, second-born son of Lothar the Great and grandson of King Clovis, died at Orléans in the thirty-third year of his reign, not without a reputation for sanctity. His kingdom passed to his cousin Hildebert by [unclear] of [unclear]. In the following year Richard, king of the Visigoths, entered into a treaty with the kings of the Franks, and took as his wife the sister of the aforesaid King Hildebert. In the same year, on the twenty-first day of the month of November, Saint Columbanus died, abbot, priest, and teacher of the Scots and Picts; he left to his successors many memorials of sanctity, except that, in rustic simplicity, he neither learned nor taught that Easter ought to be celebrated on the Lord’s day, and never on another day.

In the thirteenth year of Lothar, king of the Franks, Hildebert, king of the Franks, died at Orléans. He was the son of King Sigebert, who was the son of Lothar, who was the son of Clovis, the first Christian king. He left two sons, Theobert and Theodoric, who divided their father’s kingdom between themselves; their grandmother Brunichild sowed many kinds of dissensions among them.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s nativity 605, in the eighth Roman indiction, which was the eighteenth year of the reign of Lothar, Theodobert and Theoderic, the aforesaid brothers, stirred to fury by their grandmother Brunichild, who, as a supporter of Theoderic, labored with incredible hatred against Theodobert, waged a most savage war between themselves, in which more than thirty thousand fighting men fell. Also an angel of the Lord, holding and brandishing a drawn sword in his hand, was seen in the air above the people by many who were present.

At last Theodobert, having been defeated, since he could do nothing else, sought safety in flight. His brother Theoderic pursued him as far as Cologne Agrippina, and along the whole road ceaselessly cut down his soldiers as they fled likewise. But Theodobert entered Cologne and immediately ordered the city gates to be closed.

Theoderic, his brother, pursuing him, as has been said, encircled Cologne with a siege. The citizens, rushing to the walls, asked Theoderic for the terms of peace. He answered them: “You will never have peace from me unless first you cut off my brother’s head and throw it out to me from the wall. But if you refuse to do this, I shall not depart from here until, when the city has been violently taken, I destroy you all with your lord, your little children, and your wives.”

When they heard this, the citizens were exceedingly terrified; and after holding counsel among themselves, at last, lest it happen that all should perish, they cut off the head of King Theodobert, their lord, and threw it out over the wall to the impious Theoderic, as he had ordered, thus purchasing peace disgracefully in the blood of their own king.

The Lombards lay waste the borders of the Romans. The Cassinese monastery is destroyed by the Lombards. King Gunthram of Orléans dies. Hildebert succeeded Gunthram. The Franks enter into a treaty with the Visigoths. Saint Columbanus the abbot died. King Hildebert of Orléans dies. A most savage war takes place between the brother kings of Francia. Thirty thousand Franks perished. An angel was seen in the air with a sword. Theodobert flees from the battle to Cologne. King Theoderic pursues his brother as far as Cologne. The people of Cologne cut off the head of their own king.
King Theodoric enters Cologne after his brother has been killed.
The three sons of King Theodobert, who had been slain. One very beautiful daughter of the same man. Brunichild killed her own grandsons.
Sigebert, the king’s son, fled to the eastern [lands]. Sigebert becomes duke of the Alemanni and the Helvetians.
King Theodoric of Austrasia dies. Lothar becomes monarch of the whole kingdom of the Franks.
Brunichild, killer of ten kings, is slain.
Lothar entrusted the monarchy of the kingdom to counts. Wernher, mayor of the palace. Harpo is appointed count of Burgundy.

Thus made victor, in his brother’s blood, the savage King Theodoric entered Cologne in peace, and received the city itself and its citizens, together with his brother’s whole kingdom of the Austrasians, in surrender. He too, at last, died by the poison of his grandmother Brunichild, as we shall say in its place, having been deprived of heirs.

King Theodobert, slain by a miserable fate, left three sons and one, as is read, very beautiful daughter: namely Sigebert, Gunthram, and Lothar. I have found the name of the daughter nowhere. But King Theodoric, after entering Cologne, sent the aforesaid two younger sons of his brother, Gunthram and Lothar, and their sister as captives to the city of Metz. Their cruel grandmother Brunichild, meeting them and inflamed with excessive fury, in hatred of their slain father rushed upon them and killed with her own hand her grandsons, still little children, who [unclear].

But Sigebert, the elder son of Theodobert by birth, lowered by the help of certain citizens secretly over the wall and across the Rhine, fled in the dress of a scholar. Coming into eastern Francia, he lay hidden for some years, unknown, among his kinsmen Godfrid and his son Genebald III, dukes of the Franks, who ruled around the Main and Wurzburg. At length, after the death of King Theodoric, through the intervention of the princes, he received by the gift of King Lothar a duchy in Upper Alemannia, which is now called Helvetia; but he was not permitted either to bear the royal name or to wear the diadem according to the custom of his fathers. And he remained under the authority of the kingdom of the Franks.
He begot a son with his father’s name, Theobert.

In the thirty-first year of King Lothar, and in the six hundred eighteenth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the sixth indiction of the Romans, King Theodoric of Austrasia died at Metz by the poison of his grandmother Brunichild, in the nineteenth year of his reign. Lothar, the already mentioned son of Hilperic, received his kingdom, and so, according to the prophecy that Saint Columbanus had once foretold to him, he attained the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks, and thereafter reigned alone for thirteen years.

And on the other side, when the sons of King Theodoric, at Brunichild’s instigation, raised an army, they were defeated; and Brunichild herself, the inciter of all evils, was captured and presented to Lothar together with Eudolina, daughter of King Theodoric. Condemned by the decree of the nobles, she received the sentence of a dreadful death. For, after being mutilated in one foot and the opposite arm, and tied to the tail of an untamed mare, she was torn apart limb by limb by the violent dragging. They said that she had destroyed ten kings.

Therefore Lothar, raised to monarchy over the whole kingdom of the Franks, which had previously been divided into four, since he could not profitably govern so broad a dominion by himself alone, entrusted the provinces to counts descended from the ancient stock of kings. He appointed as count, or prefect, of the royal palace Guarnerius, a noble and very eminent man.
But Burgundy he committed to a certain Harpo to govern; he too was a count born from the most ancient line of the kings of the Franks.

Rado was appointed count of Austrasia. Genebaldus was duke of Mainz. Marcopolis is now called Wurzburg. The origin of the counts palatine and dukes of Bavaria. The Palatinate is joined to the duchy of Bavaria. Sigebertus was duke of the Franks in Alemannia. The Lombards were tributaries of the Franks. Wernher, mayor of the palace, dies. Pippin, son of Ansegil, afterward mayor of the palace. The line of descent of Charles the Great, together with the dukes of Brabant and Bavaria.

He also entrusted Austrasia to Rado, a most noble count; in it were the most renowned cities: Trier, Metz, Liege, Cologne, the Mosellan [unclear], Luxembourgers, Austrasians, [Euphalians?], Namurians, and many others.

To Genebaldus, the third of that name, duke of the Franks in the east at Marcopolis, which is now called Wurzburg from the adjacent castle of Saint Mary on the mountain, he assigned Mainz, Worms, Speyer, and the peoples of those same regions; he founded Frankfurt beside the Main.

But to Pippin, who was the son of Duke Ansegisus, brother of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and also count of Namur and duke of Brittany, from whom the counts palatine, the counts of the Rhine, and the dukes of Bavaria who live today, eighteen in number, all descended, as I know, apart from the females, on the mother's side, namely from Gertrude, daughter of Henry, count palatine dwelling at Heidelberg, who, having been married to Otto, duke of Bavaria, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1225, joined the principality of Bavaria to the Palatinate; King Lotharius assigned all Lower or northern Francia, that is, the people of Tournai, Arras, the Morini, Terouanne, Cambrai, and whatever lies between them, besides the county of Namur and the duchy of Brabant, which belonged by right to the aforesaid Ansegisus.

To Duke Sigebertus, son of the late Theodobert, king of the Franks in Austrasia, whose head, as we have said, the people of Cologne cut off, King Lotharius, after he was made duke through the intervention of the nobles, entrusted the cities of Alemannia: Chur, Lausanne, Constance, Basel, and the peoples settled around them, the Alemanni, the [Caurici?], and the Helvetii dwelling at the source of the Rhine.

In the thirty-second year of his reign, in the seventh Roman indiction, Lotharius, king of the Franks, remitted to the Lombards, after a treaty had first been made, the tribute of twelve thousand gold florins which they were obliged to pay each year to the Franks.

In the thirty-eighth year of Lotharius, king of the Franks, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, died Werner, count of the palace, or mayor of the palace of the Franks. After him Ansegil, son of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, monk and hermit, previously a married man, was made mayor of the palace of the Franks; with his son Pippin, and Saint Arnulf himself, faithfully assisting him, he held the principate. Pippin, afterward mayor of the palace, who was called the Elder, was the son of the aforesaid Ansegisus, who was son of Saint Arnulf. He was son of Ansegil, or, as others write, of Arnold the Elder. He was son of Ambertus, surnamed Nicanor, born from Blidehild, daughter of Lotharius, the first king of Clovis. That Ambertus was son of Duke Sigebertus.

He was son of Duke Priamus. He was son of Duke Heribertus. He was son of Duke Leontius. He was son of Duke Meroveus. He was son of Duke Diocles. He was son of Duke Sunno. He was son of Duke Genebaldus. He was son of Duke Dagobertus. He was son of Marcomir, king of the Franks. He was son of King Clodio. He was son of King Theodomer. He was son of King Richimer. He was son of King Clodomer. He was son of King Dagobert. He was son of King Walther. He was son of King Clodius. He was son of King Barther. He was son of King Hilderic. He was son of King Sunno. He was son of King Pharabert.
Pippin, son of Ansegil, afterward mayor of the palace.
The line of descent of Charles the Great, together with the dukes of Brabant and Bavaria.
Sigebertus was duke of the Franks in Alemannia.
Wernher, mayor of the palace, dies.
Rado was appointed count of Austrasia.
Marcopolis is now called Wurzburg.
The Palatinate is joined to the duchy of Bavaria.
The Lombards were tributaries of the Franks.

Pippin, afterward mayor of the palace, who was son of Ansegil, or, as others write, of Arnold the Elder, duke. He was son of Duke Meroveus, of Duke Diocles. He was son of Duke Dagobert, of King [Marcomir?]. He was son of King Clodio. [He was son of] King Richimer. He was son of King Clodomer.
Of the counts palatine also, at the same time.
The generation also of the counts of Namur.
All these descended from the ancient stock of the kings of the Franks down to these men.
From Marcomir to Charlemagne, fifty-four generations.
Dagobert, son of King Lothar, becomes king of Austrasia.
Arnulf, bishop of Metz. Pippin, duke.
The expedition of King Dagobert against the Saxons. Berthulf, duke of the Saxons, is killed by the Franks.
The Saxons are recalled under tribute to the Franks.
Lothar, the younger king of the Franks, dies.

Who was [son] of King Chlodomer. Who was [son] of King Marcomer. Who was [son] of King Odomar. Who was [son] of King Richimer. Who was [son] of King Rather. Who was [son] of King Antenor. Who was [son] of King Chlodomer. Who was [son] of King Marcomer. Who was [son] of King Clodio. Who was [son] of King Francus, from whom the Sicambri were first called Franks. Who was [son] of King Antharius. Who was [son] of King Cassander. Who was [son] of King Merodach. Who was [son] of King Chlodomir. Who was [son] of King Nicanor. Who was [son] of King Chlodomir. Who was [son] of King Basagot. Who was [son] of King Diocles. Who was [son] of King Helenus. Who was [son] of King Antenor. Who was [son] of King Marcomir, who led the Franks from Scythia into Germany. But Pippin the elder begot Charles Martel, and he begot Pippin the younger, mayor of the palace of the Franks, and king after Childeric. Thus from King Marcomir the first down to King Pippin, son of Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, and father of Saint Gertrude, there are counted fifty-one generations over the course of one thousand fifty-nine years.

But King Lothar, in the forty-first year of his reign, which was the six hundred and eighth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the first indiction of the Romans, appointed Dagobert, his son by Queen Bertrada, king of Austrasia, assigning to him Metz, Trier, Cologne, Liege, Tournai, Arras, Tongeren, Therouanne, the Morini, and whatever lay between the western sea, the English sea to the north also, and the Rhine. He earnestly entrusted him to Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and to Pippin, count of Namur and most noble duke of the Brabantians, to be instructed and guided. Dagobert established the seat of his kingdom, after the custom of the old kings of Austrasia, in the aforesaid city of Metz, and arranged the kingdom of the Franks well, both by himself and through dukes and counts.

In the following year the Saxons, rising in rebellion, refused the customary tribute to the Franks. Therefore King Dagobert, having gathered the forces of his men, moved his army against the rebels and waged war with Berthulf, duke of the Saxons; from the first encounter he was gravely wounded. When his father Lothar, who was then in Ardenne, heard this reported by a swift messenger, he immediately crossed the Rhine at Neuss and hastened to the aid of his son. The battle is renewed, and on both sides the fighting is hard and fierce. At last, however, the Saxons, after their duke Berthulf had been slain by the Franks, were defeated and sought safety in flight.

But King Lothar, pursuing the fugitives with the Franks, laid them low in a pitiable slaughter, sparing no one, but killing with the sword all who exceeded the length of his sword. The people, however, who had remained throughout Saxony he recalled to subjection to the Franks, and imposed on them a tribute of five hundred oxen.

After these things, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 631, in the fourth indiction of the Romans, the aforesaid Lothar, king of the Franks, died in the forty-fourth year of his reign, leaving by his wife
the first, who was called Bertrudis, [bore] a son named Dagobert, who succeeded to the kingdom. After his first wife had died, he had taken a second, named Sichildis, who bore Heribert.

Dagobert, the elder son of King Lotharius, succeeding his father in the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the Lord’s nativity noted above, reigned fourteen years; and earlier in Austrasia, as has been said, three years while his father was still living. Thus the whole time during which he reigned was seventeen years.

Heribert, however, Dagobert’s brother by his father, but born of another mother, as has been said, received in the division of the kingdom Aquitaine, Toulouse, and the other cities contained between the Pyrenees and the Loire, as the possession of his inheritance, on this condition: that in the other kingdoms of the Franks he should claim no right for himself. He established the principal seat of his kingdom at Toulouse. In the fourth year after this, when an occasion for war had been seized, he received the Gascons in surrender.

King Dagobert built the monastery of Saint Dionysius the martyr anew from the foundations, and enriched it with many estates, goods, and possessions, though not without injury to certain churches, which he despoiled by force of many ornaments, as though all things, acquired both lawfully and unlawfully, were owed to the services of blessed Dionysius. He built the church of the same monastery, altogether most beautiful, which was covered with solid silver; into it he transferred the bodies of the said martyr and his companions from the Catulian village and placed them in a golden shrine. He also most beautifully adorned the inner walls of the church with tapestries most fittingly woven with pearls and large pearls. He gave the place to be inhabited by monks of our order.

Dagobert first had a wife named Gertrude, whom he repudiated because of sterility, and he brought in another, whose name was Nanthildis. Finally he kept going to many crowds of concubines, besides those whom he maintained in several places, arrayed and adorned like queens. Yet Pippin, mayor of the palace, or count palatine, who had been duke of Brabant and at the same time count of Namur, nephew of Saint Arnulf and father of Saint Gertrude, a virgin nun at Nivelles in Brabant, resisted his shameful deeds quite considerably, and by no means allowed the king to sink so freely, according to his own will, through so many vices.

In the second year of King Dagobert, which was the six hundred thirty-third year of the Lord’s nativity, his wife Nanthildis bore him a son, who was named Sigebert. This infant, forty days old, when he was baptized by Saint Amandus the bishop, while all were silent, himself answered “Amen” in a clear voice. Heribert, his uncle, who was reigning at Toulouse, lifted this Sigebert from the holy font of baptism. But when King Heribert died after some years, and not long afterward also his son, named [unclear]
Sichildis was the mother of Heribert.
The fifty-first.
Dagobert reigned seventeen years.
Heribert, his brother, reigned in Aquitaine.
The monastery of Saint Dionysius is founded in Gaul.
The church of Saint Dionysius was covered with silver.
Queen Gertrude, being sterile, is repudiated. King Dagobert was excessively lustful.
Pippin, mayor of the palace of the Franks.
An infant of forty days, when he was baptized, answered: Amen.
The monarchy of the kingdom of the Franks is transferred to Dagobert.
With Hilperic, the monarchy of the whole kingdom of the Franks reverted to Dagobert, many always tending toward one, and again, by the plurality of sons, confounding unity.
When King Heribert had died, the Vascones refused to obey and be subject to the Franks; King Dagobert attacked them in war and compelled them to submission.

At the same time [Iudicahel?], who held the duchy of the same Armorican Brittany, terrified by the threat of imminent war, subjected himself and all the people of Armorican Brittany to Dagobert, king of the Franks, and to his successors forever. King Dagobert also attacked in war the Slavs, the Sorbs, who are now called Bohemians; he defeated and overcame them, and made them subject and tributary to the Franks.

If this Dagobert, the great king of the Franks, founded that once distinguished, exempt, and royal monastery of our order in the town of Wissembourg, in the diocese of Speyer, concerning which we have heard many expressing doubt, it seems to me that this was done in the third year after the death of his father, [unclear], since he reigned only fourteen years, although certain uncertain authors seem to have thought otherwise. With this reckoning of times agrees the number of the year of the Lord’s Nativity 634, which was the third year of the aforesaid Dagobert, but the sixth of his reign over Austrasia, and not the twentieth, as we read in the copied letters of that Dagobert himself. How shall we be able to know whether they are true or false, unless we see their archetype? Desiring to untie the knot of this doubt, let us set down a copy of the letters.

Dagobert, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks, to all the chief men of his kingdom, indeed to all professing the Christian faith, both future and present. A vow by which anyone has bound himself to God or to his saints cannot be made void without the stain of guilt; and the greater and more worthy is he to whom it is vowed, by so much heavier a judgment will the presumption of one who vows and does not pay be struck. Therefore we too ought and wish to render what we have vowed to the Lord, the terrible God, and to him who takes away the spirits of princes, terrible among all the kings of the earth. How he terrified us with the arm of his power, how, striking and healing, he visited us again, we have judged should be made known to all as an example of correction, especially so that every faithful person, having heard of our peril, may restrain himself from the devastation of the churches of God, and [unclear]; distracted, I neglected the duty of royal office, showing no solicitude or diligence toward those entrusted to me, doing or judging nothing from gentleness or zeal for justice. Among my other transgressions, the destruction of the churches of God [unclear].
King Dagobert enumerates his transgressions.
Copy of the letters of foundation of the said monastery. He makes mention of his vow. Dagobert relates that he was carried off into heaven. King Dagobert enumerates his transgressions.

and I had begun to be the destroyer of those things of which I ought to have been the defender and exalter, fearing neither the eyes of the divine majesty nor the outcry of men. At length the kindness of God, crushing the pride of my obstinate mind with the rod of correction, visited my iniquities, and, when I had been chastened, did not deny me pardon. For, caught up on high and presented before the divine majesty, seated among the choirs of the saints in the guise of one judging, I was gravely and steadfastly accused by the most holy patrons of the churches for ecclesiastical goods seized by robbery by me and consumed, especially by the most holy Mary, mother of God, and by the most blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles.

¶ And when, burdened by conscience, I did not dare to defend my offences, at length my special patron, the martyr Dionysius, came to my aid; by his prayers he obtained for me a period of delay of the punishment that was pressing upon me. He himself, as though setting a manner of penance, placed in this my hope of full pardon: if, to the honour of God and of the holy preachers whom I had more greatly offended, I should build a house suitable for divine services. Gladly making this promise, I vowed it, and, dismissed by those above, I returned. Therefore, in sure hope of remission and pardon of our sins, rendering with eager zeal all that we have done, we have built a church in honour of the Holy Trinity, and of holy Mary ever-virgin, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the place called Vuyssenburg; and we have determined to exalt it and enrich it with royal munificence. Therefore we give to it, and wish to have been given in perpetuity, from the property of our fisc lying adjacent there, whatever belongs to us, both in villages and in bondsmen, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses; and all these things we transfer by free conveyance to the use of the brethren serving God there under monastic profession. And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and firm for all time, we have taken care to note below the boundaries and the names of the surrounding places. Toward the eastern region the march which we have conveyed extends as far as Morchohouen and to Aldenherden, and thence to Goboldefvuege, and thence below Nadumlutra, and thence to Buozdigenhurst, and thence to the boundary which stands on the summit of the valley Iuuenesdal, and thence it leads toward the southern region above Vuarbach, and thence to Bodemloseffaffa, and thence to Sebach, and thence to Kirchdal, and thence to Ingoldesizahe, and thence to the wooded mountains as far as Bedebur. Toward the western region, however, as far as Lutenbach and Bernbach, and thence to Grunenbrunnen, and thence to Otterichescheyt. Toward the northern region as far as Eichenerenberg. But the place itself, which we embrace with singular devotion, now and henceforth we wish to be free from every oppression of servitude, under royal protection, namely in such a way that no public judge, no one from the judicial power, may presume to have any power there, nor to compel the men of that place either to hear cases, or to pay [auffreda?], or taxes. Finally, absolutely nothing from them
He asserts that he was presented before God judging.
Nothing is more grievous than a conscience burdened with sins.

He vowed to build a new monastery in that very rapture.
The king’s endowment for the monastery of Vuyssen.
The location of the donation toward the east.
Iuuenesdal; Busdigenhurst, a wood.

The location of the donation toward the north.

He grants the monastery coinage on the model of that of Speyer.
He wishes the men of the monastery to be free.
The monks’ freedom of choosing an abbot for themselves.
The abbot will be able to create knights for himself.
The ministerials are to obey the abbot alone.
He states the advocate’s right over the household.
